opening.headline: Agents tracing determines where to place and who can view them, and learns how evaluation results connect to operational metrics.
body: Once an agent is executed, multiple intermediate steps such as LLM calls, searches, and tool invocations are generated. Traces contain the inputs and outputs, latency, and token usage for each step. The storage location of these records determines the number of stored entries, access controls, and retrieval methods.

If evaluation results are kept separate from operational metrics, it becomes impossible to identify quality degradation issues related to delays or costs. This course compares the approach of storing Databricks MLflow traces in Unity Catalog with Snowflake's AI Observability, distinguishing what each evaluates in terms of quality and safety. Finally, it examines cases where sensitive information remains in traces from a governance perspective.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the tracing storage methods and evaluation types of Databricks and Snowflake.
Trace data retention locations and access scopes can be analyzed from a governance perspective.

screens.title: Where to store traces and how to preserve evaluation results?
screens.lead: First, let's examine what record a single agent execution leaves behind. The two question marks in the figure represent the questions this lesson aims to answer.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the span bundle created by one agent execution, along with two question boxes asking about the storage and evaluation results.

paragraphs: Each execution of an agent involves multiple intermediate steps such as LLM calls, searches, and tool invocations. Tracing includes inputs and outputs, latency, and token usage for each step. This record serves as the foundational data expected for debugging, evaluation, and operational monitoring.

However, the issue lies in where this record is stored. If it is kept only within a single experiment, it will be hindered by limits on quantity and access control. Moreover, if evaluation results—such as quality and safety scores—are kept separate from operational metrics like delays or costs, it will be impossible to trace the causes of declining quality.

This course answers two questions by comparing Databricks' trace storage approach with Snowflake's AI Observability: where will traces be stored and who will be able to view them, and how will evaluation results be preserved and documented.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: In traces, the original text entered by the user may be stored verbatim. Then, are traces merely logs, or are they data possessing permissions and retention policies? This will be revisited during the later part of the lecture.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how we are currently presenting our evaluation results.

screens.title: Are evaluation results being reported together with operational metrics?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought summary is displayed. Since no answer is entered, first recall how your environment handles this, and then try it.

items.prompt: Should response quality evaluation values, delay, and cost graphs be displayed on the same screen?
items.answer: You need to be able to see whether delays or costs changed simultaneously when quality scores decline, in order to narrow down the root cause. If evaluation results are separately available from other tools, this comparison becomes cumbersome. That's why traceability and evaluation results are kept in the same place.

items.prompt: Who can view the user input contained in the trace?
items.answer: Traces may contain the original input, so the viewing scope directly becomes the scope of personal information exposure. The granularity of control differs between granting permissions at the experimental unit level and at the table level. We must be able to specify who can view the data.

items.prompt: How long and where can retention of traces be stored?
items.answer: Without knowing the retention period and location, it is impossible to investigate old issues or respond to audits. Conversely, retaining data longer than necessary extends the period during which sensitive information remains. This course verifies how the answer varies depending on the storage location.

screens.outro: Now let's examine how Databricks records traces and where they are stored.

screens.title: Databricks: MLflow Tracking and Unity Catalog Trace Storage
screens.lead: Expand each item sequentially to check how tracing is recorded, differences in storage locations, the tables created, and the required permissions.

visual.alt: A two-pathflow diagram from the app through MLflow Tracing to an experiment repository or a Unity Catalog table.

items.title: What MLflow Tracing Records
items.body: MLflow Tracing forms the foundation of GenAI observability in Databricks. It records inputs, outputs, latency, token usage, and costs for every intermediate step of an agent, providing a complete view of the execution flow. Built using the standard MLflow SDK and OpenTelemetry, it supports traces for debugging, evaluation, and operational monitoring. Therefore, a single recorded trace can be reused across various use cases.

items.title: Constraints of the experimental repository
items.body: Traces saved within an experiment can be queried via the MLflow UI and Python SDK. However, there is a limit of 100,000 traces per experiment, and access is restricted only at the experiment level. OpenTelemetry format compatibility is not supported. While sufficient for small-scale use, the limits and access controls become constraints in operational environments.

items.title: Advantages of Unity Catalog Storage
items.body: When using Unity Catalog storage, traces are accumulated as Delta tables in OTel format. There is no limit on the number of traces, and they can be directly queried using existing tools such as SQL, Genie Code, AI/BI dashboards, and Spark-based tools. Access control is managed through Unity Catalog schema and table permissions instead of experimental-level ACLs. Note that users who can access a table can view traces from any experiment. This approach is recommended for new workloads and operational workloads.

items.title: The created tables and required permissions
items.body: When an experiment is bound to a Unity Catalog trace location, four tables are created in the schema, named `_otel_spans`, `_otel_logs`, `_otel_metrics`, and `_otel_annotations`. To write or read traces, the catalog requires `USE CATALOG`, the schema requires `USE SCHEMA`, and each table requires `MODIFY` and `SELECT`. `ALL PRIVILEGES` alone is insufficient; therefore, `MODIFY` and `SELECT` must be explicitly granted. The schema must exist first, and an experiment once bound to a trace location cannot be moved to another trace location.

screens.outro: Having examined Databricks' storage approach, let's now compare how Snowflake divides observation and evaluation.

screens.title: Two Types of Snowflake AI Observability and Evaluation
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore how the observation methods differ for each Snowflake feature, and what each evaluation is assessing.

tabs.label: Observation scope
tabs.body: Snowflake AI Observability provides a set of features that help you verify what happened during an operation request, how well the model performs on test data, the cost of the request, and whether guardrails blocked the request. Not all Cortex features support the same observation methodology. You must first check how each feature's observations are available.

tabs.label: Cortex Agents
tabs.body: Cortex Agents automatically record conversation threads and traces, which can be viewed in the Observability and Evaluations tabs of Snowsight. You can inspect real-time agent threads and traces and perform bulk evaluations on datasets. AI apps created directly can send telemetry to TruLens, regardless of whether they are running inside or outside Snowflake.

tabs.label: Built-in AI Functions and Search
tabs.body: Built-in AI functions such as AI_COMPLETE do not use tracing and instead record credits, tokens, function name, and model for each call in the Account Usage view. When request logging is enabled in Cortex Search, request-level events are logged and can be queried using `GET_AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS`. Different Cortex features use different surfaces—tracing, request logs, or usage view.

tabs.label: Quality Assessment
tabs.body: Quality evaluation performs a batch assessment of datasets to numerically evaluate response quality. It compares how accurate and appropriate the responses are when a model or agent is given a predefined set of questions with expected answers. It is used when comparing the quality of a new version against an existing version before deployment, and the results are stored as evaluation execution units.

tabs.label: Safety assessment
tabs.body: Security evaluation checks whether personally identifiable information or financial information, such as sensitive data, is present in inputs and outputs. Datadog's Sensitive Data Scanner integration identifies and masks sensitive information in prompt-response pairs within LLM applications. While quality evaluation assesses whether an answer is appropriate, security evaluation examines whether the answer and question contain hazardous content.

screens.outro: Having compared the two platforms' approaches, let's now apply this to a single case and explore the governance settings.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Sensitive Information Remaining in Traces and Governance Settings
screens.lead: The instructor walks through a step-by-step analysis of a case where a customer service agent's trace contains a resident registration number. Select the following arrow to proceed in order: discovery, meaning, storage location, reduction, and operational connection.

visual.alt: Diagram showing the process where sensitive columns in the trace table change from original, detection flag, and obscured values, and readable permission lists decrease.

steps.title: Situation: The resident registration number is directly entered in the input field.
steps.body: The customer service agent's trace input field contains the customer's stated resident number and card number exactly as entered. The trace feature designed to improve customer service quality has instead become a repository for sensitive information.

steps.title: Stage 1 Discovery: Safety assessment indicates it.
steps.body: Security assessment, or sensitive information detection, identifies personal information patterns in inputs and outputs. This evaluation mechanism detects such exposures without requiring a person to manually inspect them. The assessment result only indicates a problem—it does not correct the issue.

steps.title: Stage 2 meaning: Traces are also data
steps.body: Trace data is also data. At the moment the original input is stored, that record becomes a governance object with defined storage location, access scope, and retention period. We must move beyond the notion that logs are merely logs and begin by defining who can access the data and from where.

steps.title: Step 3: Organize storage locations and permissions
steps.body: Store traces in a Unity Catalog schema and grant table read permissions only to the necessary groups. For example, restrict read access to a group like `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.mlflow_traces.my_otel_spans TO trace_readers;`. Assign write privileges to `MODIFY` and `SELECT`, and grant catalog and schema access to `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA`. By limiting read access to the trace table, all experiment traces will be visible, so read permissions should be narrowly scoped.

steps.title: Step 4: Reduce by hiding before saving
steps.body: The safest sensitive information is information that is not stored. Obfuscate inputs or exclude fields before storage. Then, re-run the evaluation tool to verify that the obfuscated values are actually applied. Integrations such as Datadog's Sensitive Data Scanner help identify and obfuscate sensitive information in prompt-response pairs.

steps.title: Step 5: Operational Connection – Review Evaluation Results Together
steps.body: Configure the evaluation results to be queried alongside delay and cost indicators within a table-based structure such as trace, so that you can simultaneously see which models or call paths increased when warnings arose during security evaluations.

steps.title: Conclusion: The same trace becomes verifiable data.
steps.body: By defining storage location, access permissions, and retention period, the same trace becomes debugging data that is also auditable. If not defined, the same trace becomes a pathway for exposure of sensitive information.

screens.outro: We have completed the example. Now, I will summarize the content discussed so far.

screens.title: Core takeaway: Traces are data and are subject to governance.
screens.lead: We summarize the course content by comparing the two platforms from a governance perspective. Review the first two questions as you read.

paragraphs: Start with storage location organization. Databricks stores traces in Unity Catalog tables, which can be queried via SQL and have access scopes controlled through schema and table permissions. Experimentation storage has a limit of 100,000 items per experiment and is governed by experiment units, so for operational scale, storing in Unity Catalog is recommended. Table access requires USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and MODIFY and SELECT privileges.

Snowflake has different observation surfaces depending on the feature. Cortex Agents provide traces and evaluations in Snowsight, built-in AI functions show usage in the Account Usage view, and custom apps send telemetry via TruLens. First, confirm that the available views differ based on the feature being used.

Evaluation is divided into two types. Quality evaluation assesses how good the response is, while safety evaluation checks whether sensitive information is present in the inputs and outputs. Regardless of the platform, traces may contain the original input, so defining retention locations, access permissions, and retention periods marks the beginning of governance. If these three aspects can be addressed, traces can be confidently accumulated.

callout.label: Go back to the first question
callout.text: Traces are not merely logs; they are data with assigned permissions and retention policies. By evaluating trace results alongside operational metrics within the same system, one can identify the root causes of quality issues.

checks.q: What is an appropriate advantage of storing traces in Databricks' Unity Catalog?
options: Traces are accumulated in Delta tables and queried via SQL, controlled by schema and table permissions.
The trace limit of 100,000 per experiment is applied as is.
With only ALL PRIVILEGES, both reading and writing are possible.
Governance is only achieved through experimental-level access control.
checks.explain: UC storage accumulates traces in OTel-format delta tables, enabling SQL queries, and enforces governance through schema and table permissions.

wrong.2: ALL PRIVILEGES alone is not sufficient; USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, MODIFY, and SELECT are required.

Cortex Agents records traces, while AI_COMPLETE only retains usage data.
AI_COMPLETE only can view traces in the Evaluations tab.

glossary.def: Databricks' tracing feature records step-by-step inputs, outputs, delays, tokens, and costs of agent execution.
This approach stores traces in Delta tables in OTel format, enabling unlimited SQL queries and controlling access through schema and table permissions.
Snowflake's observability events that record Cortex feature traces and events.
A tool that sends telemetry from directly built AI apps to a Snowflake account.
An assessment that checks whether sensitive information, such as personal or financial data, is present in inputs or outputs.

misconceptions.myth: Tracing is merely logging and has no relation to data governance.
misconceptions.fact: Trace contains original input data that requires specification of storage location, viewing permissions, and retention period.

misconceptions.myth: Granting ALL PRIVILEGES allows access to the trace table.
misconceptions.fact: The trace table requires explicit grants for MODIFY and SELECT. Grants for USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are also necessary.

misconceptions.myth: Snowflake's entire AI functionality generates traces in the same manner.
misconceptions.fact: Each functionality has a different observation surface. Cortex Agents use traces, built-in AI functions use usage views, and custom apps verify through TruLens.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Traces are data and are subject to governance.
Unity Catalog storage provides SQL queries, schema, and table permissions with no quantity limits.
Snowflake has different observation surfaces for each feature, and its built-in AI functions can be verified through usage views.
Quality assessment examines response quality, while safety assessment reviews sensitive information.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where is my trace stored, for how long, who can access it, and what sensitive information does it contain?
